The honest caveat he's given himself is that this logic has a shelf life, he's been fairly candid in shareholder letters that as Berkshire has grown enormous, finding new opportunities large enough to meaningfully move the needle has gotten harder, which is an implicit acknowledgment that the same no-dividend argument gets weaker as the pool of retained capital grows relative to the available high-return opportunities.
That's a fair distinction actually, track record versus just asserting it. Do you think Berkshire will eventually have to start paying one once Buffett isn't running it?

It's a reasonable prediction, and quite a few observers of the company have floated it for similar reasons. The no-dividend policy has always been sustainable specifically because there was strong confidence in the capital allocator's ability to keep finding attractive uses for the cash, and that confidence was built directly on Buffett's individual track record and reputation over an extraordinarily long career. Once leadership transitions to whoever succeeds him, even a highly capable successor, that same level of accumulated trust doesn't transfer automatically, it has to be earned freshly, and in the meantime shareholders and the market may be less patient about large amounts of cash sitting retained without a similarly storied allocator at the helm to justify it. That dynamic, more than any change in the underlying financial logic, is probably what would eventually push a future Berkshire toward returning cash directly to shareholders, not because the reinvestment principle stopped being sound in theory, but because the specific trust that made it credible in practice was personal to one person's results.

My alma mater has this massive endowment, in the billions, and yet they're always doing fundraising drives for basic stuff. Why don't they just spend more of the endowment every year instead of constantly asking alumni for more money?

It feels counterintuitive, but there's a deliberate structural reason behind it, and it's similar in spirit to how a company manages a long-term payout it wants to sustain indefinitely rather than draw down. Most university endowments operate under a spending policy that intentionally caps annual withdrawals at a modest percentage of the fund's value, commonly somewhere in the range of four to five percent, specifically because the goal is for the endowment to exist in perpetuity, supporting the institution not just this year but a century from now, adjusted for whatever inflation and growth happens along the way. If a university spent a much larger share every year, it would boost funding in the short term but would shrink the real, inflation-adjusted value of the endowment over time, eventually leaving future students and faculty with a much smaller cushion than current ones enjoy, which conflicts with the whole premise of an endowment as an intergenerational resource rather than a one-time windfall to be consumed.
Okay that makes sense for the endowment itself, but then why do the ongoing fundraising drives feel disconnected from that, like they're going after totally different pots of money?

They largely are different pots, and that's actually the source of the disconnect you're noticing. The endowment's restrained annual spending typically covers a defined, recurring slice of the university's budget, things like a portion of financial aid, endowed faculty chairs, maintenance of specific funds donors set up for particular purposes, often with legal restrictions on exactly what that money can be used for, since many large gifts come with donor-specified conditions attached rather than being free for the university to spend however it wants. Ongoing fundraising drives, by contrast, are usually targeting new capital projects, a new building, a new program, or unrestricted operating funds the university can deploy flexibly for whatever current needs arise, which the endowment's restricted, conservatively managed structure isn't well suited to cover. So it's less that the university is being stingy with a giant pile of cash sitting around, and more that most of that pile is legally earmarked or structurally protected for specific long-term purposes, leaving a real ongoing need for fresh, flexible money.
That's actually a much more sympathetic picture than I had going in. Does the same restrained-payout logic apply to like, family trusts and inheritance funds too, or is that a totally separate thing?

The underlying principle genuinely does show up in family trusts as well, and it's really the same core tension, balancing current beneficiaries' desire for income now against preserving the fund's real value for future beneficiaries or generations. Trust documents very often specify a payout rate or formula for exactly this reason, to prevent a current beneficiary from draining the principal and leaving nothing for whoever comes after them, and trustees have a formal fiduciary duty to balance those competing interests rather than simply favoring whoever is asking loudest in the present moment. The specific percentages and mechanisms differ, and family trusts have a lot more variety in structure since they're privately negotiated documents rather than following a fairly standardized nonprofit convention, but the philosophical throughline, protecting a fund's ability to keep supporting people indefinitely rather than treating it as a spendable lump sum, is essentially the same idea showing up in a more personal, family-scale context.

I'm helping design a personal finance elective for high schoolers at my kid's school and we're stuck on how much, if any, corporate/business finance concepts to include versus just keeping it to personal budgeting and saving. What's your take on that balance?

I'd lean toward keeping the bulk of the course anchored in personal finance, budgeting, credit, saving, basic investing concepts, since that's what almost every student will need to actually navigate regardless of their eventual career, but I do think a light, conceptual layer of business finance is worth including, mainly because it makes the personal-finance material more concrete rather than as a separate subject to master. For instance, when teaching students about investing in stocks, it helps enormously for them to understand at a basic level what a share of a company actually represents, ownership in a business that generates profit and sometimes distributes some of it back to owners, rather than treating a stock ticker as an abstract number that goes up and down for mysterious reasons. That kind of grounding doesn't require teaching them to analyze financial statements, just enough conceptual literacy that investing feels connected to real businesses rather than feeling like gambling on symbols.
That's a good distinction. Are there specific business concepts you'd actually flag as worth a dedicated lesson versus ones that are more advanced-elective territory?

A few concepts earn their place because they show up constantly in everyday life even for people who never work in finance professionally. Understanding basic supply and demand pricing dynamics is worth a lesson, since it explains everything from surge pricing on rideshare apps to why concert tickets and sneakers get resold above face value, and it demystifies pricing decisions students encounter constantly as consumers. A basic conceptual overview of what a company's profit versus revenue actually means is also valuable, since a lot of adults conflate the two their entire lives, thinking a company with huge sales figures must be enormously profitable when the reality is often much thinner margins after costs. I'd hold off on anything requiring real quantitative modeling, discounted cash flow analysis, detailed financial statement forecasting, that kind of depth is genuinely advanced-elective or college-level territory, and trying to compress it into a general high school course risks losing students on math mechanics rather than building the intuition you're actually going for.
Would you include something on how businesses decide to pay employees bonuses versus raises, or is that too niche for this audience?

I wouldn't build a whole dedicated lesson around it, but it's a nice concrete example to weave into a broader discussion of how businesses think about costs and incentives, since a lot of students will encounter this distinction firsthand in their very first jobs. The general intuition worth conveying is that a raise is a permanent, compounding commitment, it recurs every year and typically grows the base for future raises too, while a bonus is a one-time, more easily adjustable payment tied to results in a specific period, which gives an employer flexibility to reward good years without locking in a permanent cost increase during leaner ones. That's a genuinely useful thing for a teenager entering the workforce to understand intuitively, since it explains why a company might be generous with a bonus in a strong year while being cautious about base pay increases, and it helps set realistic expectations about negotiating compensation later without requiring any deep dive into corporate financial planning.

Got absolutely gouged by surge pricing on a rideshare last night, paid like three times the normal fare leaving a concert. I get the supply and demand logic but it still feels predatory somehow. Am I wrong to feel that way?

You're not wrong to feel that way even if the underlying mechanism is defensible in the abstract, those two things can both be true at once. The economic logic is straightforward, when a huge number of people want a ride at the same moment and there aren't enough drivers nearby, some price mechanism has to ration the limited supply, and raising prices does two useful things simultaneously, it discourages some riders from requesting a car who could just as easily walk a bit or wait it out, and it incentivizes more drivers in the area to turn on the app and head toward the surge zone, which actually does increase available supply within a fairly short window. Where the predatory feeling comes from is less about the logic itself and more about the power imbalance in the moment, you're standing outside a venue at midnight with genuinely limited alternatives, and a company is extracting the maximum price the moment leaves you willing to pay, which feels categorically different from a shortage happening in a market where you have real time and options to shop around.
Do surge multipliers actually pull in more drivers in real time like they claim, or is that just corporate spin to justify charging more?

There's genuine evidence it does work at least partially as claimed, though 'as much as claimed' is doing some work in that sentence, since the effect is real but probably smaller and slower than the cleanest version of the pitch suggests. Studies and internal data these companies have published over the years do show driver supply responding to surge signals, drivers turning the app on, or navigating toward a surging area, when multipliers spike, so it's not pure fiction. The skepticism is fair on a couple of fronts though, the response isn't instantaneous, a driver fifteen minutes away seeing a surge alert still takes fifteen minutes to arrive, so in the acute moment right when demand spikes, much of what the surge multiplier is doing in practice is rationing existing demand down rather than conjuring new supply up quickly enough to matter for people already waiting. There's also a fair critique that the exact multiplier calculation isn't transparent to riders, so there's no way to independently verify whether a given 3x charge reflects a genuinely tight market at that moment versus the algorithm being tuned in ways that favor higher company revenue during predictably busy periods like a concert letting out.
That lack of transparency is honestly the part that bugs me most. Is there any regulatory pushback on that anywhere, or is it just an unregulated wild west everywhere?

It's not a complete wild west, there has been some regulatory attention, though it's patchy and varies a lot by jurisdiction rather than being a unified global standard. Some cities and regions have introduced caps on how high a surge multiplier can go during specific circumstances, particularly during declared emergencies, since price spikes during evacuations or severe weather events draw much sharper public and political backlash than routine nightlife surges, and a few jurisdictions have general price-gouging statutes that get invoked during declared emergencies specifically. Outside of emergency situations though, garden-variety demand surges like a concert or a holiday rush are mostly left to market mechanisms with far less regulatory intervention, since regulators have generally been more cautious about capping ordinary dynamic pricing, partly out of concern that capping it too aggressively would just mean fewer available rides rather than cheaper ones, since drivers would have less incentive to be available during the exact periods riders need them most.

My company announced layoffs the same month the CEO got a huge bonus tied to hitting performance targets. Everyone I know is furious about it. Is there ever a legitimate defense of that kind of timing, or is it just as bad as it looks?

There can be a legitimate defense in principle, though whether it applies to your specific situation is something only someone with the actual numbers could judge fairly. The structural argument is that executive bonus targets are typically set at the start of a performance period, often a full year in advance, based on goals the board and executive agreed to at that time, and the metrics involved, cost efficiency, margin improvement, hitting a specific financial target, are sometimes achieved precisely through the kind of workforce reduction that later triggers layoffs. In that framing, the bonus isn't a reward disconnected from the layoffs, it's literally compensating the executive for delivering the outcome that made the layoffs 'necessary' from the company's perspective, which is at least internally consistent even if it feels morally uncomfortable from the employee side of that same decision. Where it becomes harder to defend is when the bonus reflects a broad, generic performance metric that had nothing to do with the layoffs at all, and the timing is just an unfortunate coincidence of two board decisions landing in the same reporting period, versus a case where the bonus structure and layoff decision are causally the same underlying action viewed from two different angles.
How would an outside employee or even a shareholder even tell the difference between those two scenarios from the outside?

It's genuinely hard, and that difficulty is itself part of why this kind of announcement generates so much anger, the information asymmetry means employees are left to assume the worst, often correctly. The most accessible clue for a shareholder, and sometimes an employee if the company is transparent internally, is looking at the proxy statement or compensation disclosure that publicly traded companies are required to file, which typically breaks down exactly which metrics triggered the bonus payout, cost reduction, revenue growth, stock price performance, and so on. If cost reduction or margin improvement is explicitly listed as a driver of that year's bonus, that's a fairly direct signal the layoffs likely contributed mechanically to the payout. If the bonus was driven by something like overall revenue growth or a stock price hurdle unrelated to headcount, the coincidence of timing is more plausibly just two separate decisions landing in the same news cycle rather than one causing the other. Most employees reasonably don't have the patience or access to dig through a compensation filing in the moment they're absorbing news of a friend's layoff, which is exactly why the emotional read defaults to assuming the worst version of the story.

That's a fair point about most people not digging into filings in the moment. Do you think companies should be required to disclose that connection more directly, like right there in the layoff announcement itself?

There's a reasonable case for it, though it runs into some practical friction that explains why it isn't standard practice already. From a pure transparency standpoint, requiring a company to explicitly state in a layoff announcement whether executive compensation that period was tied to the same cost metrics the layoffs were meant to improve would give employees and the public a much more direct, immediate way to judge the situation, rather than relying on people connecting the dots between a separate proxy filing and a separate layoff press release months apart. The friction is that compensation structures are often genuinely complex, tied to multiple metrics with different weightings, so a simple yes-or-no disclosure risks being either misleadingly reductive or so caveated it loses the clarity it was meant to provide. It's also the kind of disclosure companies would predictably resist adding voluntarily, since it invites exactly the scrutiny and anger you're describing, so it would likely require a regulatory mandate rather than emerging from companies choosing to be more forthcoming on their own, and that kind of specific disclosure requirement isn't something regulators have prioritized so far relative to other compensation transparency rules already in place.

My uncle runs a mid-size family manufacturing business and none of his kids want to take it over, they all went into totally different careers. He's kind of in denial about it. What are families in that situation usually supposed to do?

That situation is extremely common, actually, estimates vary but a large share of family businesses never successfully pass to a next generation for exactly this reason, interests and career paths diverging, so your uncle is far from alone even if it feels like a uniquely painful problem within his own family. The families that navigate it best tend to separate two questions that often get tangled together emotionally, whether the business itself should continue existing in some form, and whether it specifically needs to stay in the family's hands to do so. Once those get separated, several real options open up that don't require a reluctant child to take over against their wishes, bringing in an outside professional manager to run day-to-day operations while the family retains ownership and a board-level role, selling to another company in the same industry, or arranging an employee-led buyout where longtime trusted managers take over operational control, sometimes with family members staying on as passive owners collecting a share of profits rather than running things themselves.
The employee buyout idea is interesting, has that actually worked well in practice for other family businesses, or does it usually fall apart?

It has a genuinely mixed track record, and the difference between the ones that work and the ones that fall apart tends to come down to how early the planning starts and how realistic the valuation and financing structure are. The ones that go well typically begin the transition years in advance, giving the incoming employee-owners time to build up both the operational confidence and, just as importantly, the financial capacity to actually buy in gradually rather than needing to come up with the full purchase price all at once, sometimes structured so the departing family takes payments over time rather than one lump sum, which also has the side benefit of keeping the outgoing owner financially invested in the company's continued success rather than walking away indifferent to what happens next. The ones that fall apart tend to rush the timeline, often because the triggering event is the owner's sudden health issue or unplanned retirement rather than deliberate planning, and the new owners end up over-leveraged or under-prepared for the parts of running a business that a longtime owner-family had absorbed informally over decades without ever writing it down anywhere.

That point about knowledge never being written down really resonates, my uncle definitely runs things by instinct with 40 years of relationships in his head. Is there anything a family can realistically do about that specific problem before a transition happens?

Yes, and it's honestly one of the more tractable parts of succession planning precisely because it doesn't require resolving the emotionally fraught ownership question first, it can start well before anyone has decided who, if anyone, takes over. The practical approach is treating the owner's undocumented knowledge as a project in itself, systematically capturing the relationships, informal processes, and judgment calls that exist only in his head, who the key suppliers and customers actually are and what makes each relationship work, which decisions he makes on gut feel that could be turned into at least a rough documented guideline, which employees quietly hold critical institutional knowledge themselves that nobody has ever asked to write anything down. Bringing in even a junior operations hire specifically tasked with shadowing him and documenting this over a year or two, well before any ownership transition is finalized, dramatically de-risks whatever the eventual outcome turns out to be, whether that's a family member stepping in after all, an employee buyout, or an outside sale, since a business that isn't entirely dependent on one person's memory is more resilient and, frankly, more valuable under any of those paths.

I got into a debate with a coworker about whether corporate tax rates have gone up or down over the decades. He insists companies pay way less now than they used to, I thought it was roughly the same. Who's closer to right?

Your coworker has the stronger case, at least looking at statutory rates over the long arc of the past several decades in most developed economies, including the US. Top corporate tax rates were considerably higher through the mid-20th century in a lot of countries, and there's been a fairly steady downward trend since roughly the 1980s, driven by a combination of domestic policy choices and international tax competition, countries lowering rates partly to attract corporate headquarters and investment away from higher-tax jurisdictions, which then pressures other countries to follow suit to avoid losing that competitiveness, a dynamic some economists have described as a race to the bottom. That said, your instinct that things might be 'roughly the same' isn't entirely without merit if you're thinking about effective tax rates rather than statutory ones, since the actual share of profit companies pay after deductions, credits, and various planning strategies has always been meaningfully lower than the headline statutory rate, and that gap between statutory and effective rates has existed throughout the period, it's not purely a modern phenomenon.
What's actually driven that gap between the statutory rate and what companies really pay, has that gotten a lot worse recently or was it always pretty wide?

The gap has existed for a long time, but there's decent evidence it has widened further in recent decades due to a few compounding factors rather than staying constant. Multinational companies have had increasing ability to shift where profits are recognized for tax purposes, structuring operations so that profit gets attributed to lower-tax jurisdictions even when the actual economic activity, sales, production, customers, happens elsewhere, a practice that became considerably easier as businesses grew more digital and less tied to physical, geographically fixed operations that are harder to relocate on paper. Depreciation rules and various investment incentives have also become more generous over time in a lot of jurisdictions, letting companies defer or reduce taxable income by accelerating how quickly they write off capital investments, which lowers the effective rate without technically touching the statutory number at all. There's been some pushback on the profit-shifting piece specifically, international coordination efforts aimed at setting a global minimum effective corporate tax rate to reduce the incentive for that kind of jurisdiction shopping, though how effectively that gets enforced varies a lot and it's still a fairly young effort relative to how entrenched the underlying practices are.
Do you think that global minimum tax effort will actually hold up long-term or is it likely to erode the same way past reform attempts have?

It's genuinely uncertain, and there's real basis for skepticism given how past reform efforts have played out, but there are also some structural differences this time that make total erosion less of a foregone conclusion. Historically, unilateral efforts by individual countries to close loopholes have often just pushed the profit-shifting activity toward whichever other jurisdiction hadn't closed the same loophole yet, which is exactly the race-to-the-bottom dynamic that created the problem in the first place, so a single country acting alone was never going to solve something inherently international in nature. What's different about the more coordinated multi-country minimum tax approach is that it's trying to remove the incentive to relocate rather than trying to police where profit gets booked, if every major economy applies broadly similar minimum effective rates, there's less of a lower-tax haven left to shift profits toward, at least among the countries that actually sign on and enforce it. The realistic risk isn't that the whole framework collapses outright, it's more that a meaningful number of smaller jurisdictions decline to participate or find carve-outs and exceptions that keep some version of the old dynamic alive at a smaller scale, which would blunt the effort's impact without necessarily destroying it entirely.

A buddy of mine started a small craft brewery a few years back and it's actually taking off now, but he's telling me scaling up is way harder than starting the thing was in the first place. Is that a common experience or is he just having a rough go of it specifically?

That's an extremely common experience, to the point that it's practically a defined phase in how small manufacturing and food and beverage businesses tend to develop, sometimes informally called the messy middle, where the scrappy improvisation that got a business off the ground stops working and hasn't yet been replaced by the more formal systems a larger operation needs. In brewing specifically, the jump from a small batch operation to meeting real regional demand often means confronting equipment limits all at once, a fermentation setup sized for a taproom's needs simply can't produce at the volume distribution to stores and bars requires, so it's not usually a gradual scaling curve, it's a series of discrete, expensive equipment jumps that each come with their own learning curve for consistency at the new scale. On top of the physical production side, there's a whole layer of business complexity that a founder running a small taproom didn't need to think about, distributor relationships, more complex logistics and inventory management, and often navigating a much thicker web of state-by-state alcohol distribution regulation than a local taproom ever touches.
The consistency thing is interesting, why would going bigger make the beer less consistent instead of more, you'd think a bigger operation would be more precise if anything.

It's a fair intuition, but the reality tends to run the opposite direction, at least during the transition period, for a couple of concrete reasons. Small batch brewing often relies heavily on a brewer's direct sensory judgment, tasting and adjusting by feel at each stage, which works fine at a scale where one person can closely monitor every batch, but doesn't translate directly to larger equipment where the same recipe can behave differently due to changes in things like fermentation vessel geometry, temperature gradients across a much larger tank, or longer transfer times between stages that expose the beer to more opportunities for subtle variation or contamination. Larger equipment absolutely can achieve more precision than small batch gear eventually, better temperature control systems, more consistent automated processes, but only once the brewery has actually calibrated the new equipment through real experience, which typically means a string of batches that come out slightly different from the beloved original recipe while the team relearns how their product behaves at the new scale, an uncomfortable phase for a brewery whose whole reputation was built on a specific flavor profile customers already love and notice if it shifts.
That makes sense. Any general advice you'd pass along to him for navigating that phase, or is it just something you have to grind through?

There's some grinding through that's genuinely unavoidable, but a few practices seem to meaningfully shorten the painful part based on how other breweries have handled it. Running the new, larger equipment in parallel with the old small-batch setup for a while, rather than switching over all at once, gives the team a known-good baseline to compare against while dialing in the new process, and it also means a batch that comes out slightly off at the new scale doesn't threaten the entire supply if the smaller line is still producing reliably in the meantime. It's also worth being transparent with the most loyal customers and accounts during this stretch rather than pretending everything is seamless, craft beer audiences in particular tend to be understanding, and even a little charmed, by an honest 'we're scaling up and dialing in the new system, here's what to expect' message, compared to customers noticing an unexplained quality dip and quietly losing trust without ever being told why. Finally, bringing in outside expertise, even briefly, someone who has specifically navigated that same equipment jump at other breweries, tends to be worth the cost many times over compared to purely learning through trial and error, since a lot of the failure modes at that scale are well known within the industry even if they're a first-time surprise to any individual brewery going through it.

My friend who owns a small retail shop just got hit with a pretty steep rent increase notice from her landlord and she's dreading the renewal conversation. Any general advice on how small business owners should approach negotiating something like that?

The first thing worth doing before any conversation happens is gathering some outside context rather than negotiating purely from an emotional reaction to the number, specifically finding out what comparable retail spaces in the same immediate area are actually renting for right now, since that gives her an objective anchor to push back with rather than just arguing that the increase feels unfair in the abstract. It's also worth her thinking honestly about the landlord's own incentives here, a landlord generally would rather keep a reliable, established tenant who pays on time and takes care of the space than deal with vacancy risk and the real cost of finding and onboarding a new tenant, lost rent during the vacancy, marketing the space, sometimes needing to offer a new tenant concessions to sign at all. That leverage is genuinely real even for a small shop, and it's worth her walking in prepared to gently remind the landlord of the value of continuity, rather than assuming she has no negotiating power just because she's a small tenant facing a bigger landlord or property management company.
Is it better for her to push back hard on the number itself, or try to negotiate other terms instead, like the length of the lease or who covers maintenance costs?

Often the more productive path is broadening the negotiation beyond the headline rent number rather than treating it as a single number to fight over, since landlords sometimes have more flexibility on the surrounding terms than on the base figure itself, especially if the base rent increase is tied to something the landlord has less discretion over, like their own mortgage costs or property tax reassessment. Locking in a longer lease term in exchange for a smaller annual increase can be a genuine win for both sides, she gets more predictability and a lower effective rate over the life of the lease, and the landlord gets reduced vacancy risk and turnover costs locked in for longer, which is valuable to them in its own right. Similarly, negotiating who covers specific maintenance or common-area costs, or getting a period of reduced rent for a few months to offset a big jump, sometimes called a step-up structure, phasing the new higher rent in gradually rather than all at once, can make a large increase much more digestible without the landlord having to back down on the total number they're ultimately trying to get to.
The step-up idea is smart, I hadn't thought of that. Should she get anything specific in writing beyond just the usual lease terms to protect herself, given retail can be unpredictable?

Yes, a few specific protections are worth prioritizing precisely because retail foot traffic and sales can swing for reasons entirely outside her control, road construction out front, a nearby anchor tenant closing, that sort of thing. A cap on how much future increases can be, sometimes negotiated as a maximum percentage per year for the remainder of the lease term, protects her from a repeat of this exact situation happening again unpredictably down the road. If the landlord owns other units or the broader property, some form of exclusivity or non-compete clause preventing a directly competing business from opening in the same complex during her lease is also worth pursuing, since that kind of protection is easy to overlook when focused purely on the rent number but can matter enormously to her actual revenue. Finally, a clearly defined process and timeline for handling maintenance requests or property issues in writing avoids a situation where informal goodwill with the landlord quietly erodes over time and issues that used to get fixed quickly start languishing once the relationship feels more transactional after a contentious renewal negotiation.

My small business partner wants to start a profit-sharing program for our dozen employees as a way to boost morale, but I'm worried it'll just create resentment if a bad year means people get nothing after getting used to a payout. Are we overthinking this?

You're not overthinking it, that specific concern, employees anchoring on a good year's payout and then feeling a genuine loss when a leaner year produces little or nothing, is one of the most well-documented pitfalls of profit-sharing programs, and it's worth designing around explicitly rather than discovering it the hard way after a few cycles. The behavioral pattern at play is that people tend to feel a loss much more acutely than they appreciate an equivalent gain, so a program that pays out generously in good years and drops to near zero in bad ones can end up net negative for morale over time compared to no program at all, even though the average payout across those years might look perfectly reasonable on paper. A few structural choices can blunt this, communicating clearly from the very first payout that the amount is explicitly tied to that specific year's results and will vary meaningfully year to year, rather than letting a strong first year silently set an implicit expectation, and considering a smoothing mechanism, like basing the payout on a rolling average of the last two or three years' profit rather than the most recent year alone, so a single bad year doesn't cause the whole payout to collapse to zero all at once.
The rolling average idea sounds smart but wouldn't that just delay the pain into a good year, since a strong year would get dragged down by remembering a bad one from before?

That's a sharp observation, and it's the real tradeoff with smoothing, you're not eliminating the underlying variability in the business, you're redistributing when and how sharply employees feel it, which comes with real costs of its own. A rolling average genuinely does mean that a strong current year's payout gets muted somewhat by a weaker prior year still sitting in the average, and employees who understand the mechanism might reasonably feel shortchanged in that scenario, watching the company clearly do well while their payout lags behind what a pure current-year formula would have given them. The honest tradeoff is between two different risks, sharp swings that feel jarring and unpredictable year to year, versus smoother but slightly muted payouts that can feel disconnected from the company's actual current performance in either direction. Some businesses split the difference by using a mostly-current-year formula with only a modest smoothing weight toward the prior year or two, rather than a full multi-year average, which keeps the program feeling responsive to actual current results while still taking some of the sharpest edge off a single unusually bad or unusually good year.

That partial-smoothing idea seems like the right compromise for us honestly. Should we set any kind of floor or guaranteed minimum, or does that defeat the whole point of it being tied to actual profit?

A guaranteed floor does tend to weaken the core purpose of the program if it's set too generously, since the whole point of profit sharing is to genuinely connect employee reward to business outcomes rather than functioning as disguised base pay, and a floor that's high enough to always trigger regardless of performance basically converts the program into exactly that. That said, a very small, purely symbolic floor, something more like a token acknowledgment payment in a genuinely bad year rather than a meaningful chunk of typical payouts, can serve a different purpose worth considering, it signals to employees that the company values their contribution and effort even in a year the business itself struggled for reasons outside anyone's control, market conditions, a bad harvest if you're weather-exposed, whatever it might be, which helps preserve goodwill and trust in the program's fairness rather than employees feeling like a rough year for the business is being taken out entirely on their compensation. The key design principle either way is making sure the floor, if you include one at all, stays small enough relative to a typical good-year payout that employees never lose the sense that real performance genuinely drives the bulk of what they receive.

A friend of mine is launching a crowdfunding campaign for a small tabletop game and is agonizing over what dollar goal to set as the funding target. Too low and it looks unambitious, too high and it might never get reached and look like a failure. Any general wisdom on how creators should think about that?

The general wisdom that experienced crowdfunding creators converge on is to set the stated goal at the bare minimum needed to actually deliver the core product, rather than at some more aspirational number reflecting everything they'd love to include if funding went really well. The reasoning is mostly psychological and momentum-driven rather than purely financial, campaigns that reach and exceed their goal early tend to build visible social proof, other potential backers see a campaign that's already succeeded and feel more comfortable joining what looks like a sure thing, while a campaign that's crawling toward a large goal slowly, especially in its first few days, tends to lose potential backers who interpret slow momentum as a sign the project might not happen at all and don't want to risk money on something uncertain. Setting the goal at true minimum viable cost, then using stretch goals to capture the upside of a campaign that takes off, gives your friend the best of both, an achievable-looking target that's likely to hit 100 percent quickly, and a mechanism to keep momentum and excitement going afterward rather than the campaign feeling 'done' the moment the goal is technically met.
That's a good reframe. How does she figure out the actual minimum number though, like what should realistically go into that calculation for a physical product like a board game?

For a physical product like a tabletop game, the minimum viable number needs to account for a handful of costs that are easy to underestimate if she's only thinking about manufacturing per unit. The obvious piece is manufacturing cost at whatever quantity she's committing to produce, but that per-unit number usually assumes a minimum order quantity from a manufacturer, so she needs a realistic estimate of backer count to know which pricing tier she'd actually be quoted, rather than assuming the cheapest large-volume rate before she has any idea how many backers to expect. Beyond manufacturing, shipping and fulfillment for a board game specifically tends to be a much bigger and more frequently underestimated cost than new creators expect, games are heavy and awkwardly shaped compared to a lot of other crowdfunded product categories, and international shipping in particular can eat a shockingly large chunk of a naive budget if it isn't priced out carefully in advance. She should also budget for the platform's own fees plus payment processing fees taken off the top of whatever is raised, and set aside a real contingency buffer for the near-universal experience of at least one unexpected cost showing up somewhere between funding and actually delivering the physical product to backers, tooling changes, a shipping rate increase, a component that turns out to cost more once a real manufacturing quote comes in versus an early estimate.

That's a reasonable worry to hold in the back of her mind, but in practice it's a much smaller risk than the alternative of setting the goal too high and struggling to reach it, and there's a simple way to defuse it almost entirely if it does come up. A modest, achievable goal only reads as suspicious to backers when the campaign page itself feels thin or vague about how that number was actually derived, so the fix isn't raising the target, it's being transparent in the campaign description about how the minimum was calculated, showing backers she's thought seriously about manufacturing minimums, shipping, and fees rather than just picking a comfortable-sounding round number out of the air. A campaign that clearly shows its cost-of-goods thinking tends to read as more credible and well-prepared to a skeptical backer than one with a large, impressive-sounding goal that offers no visible reasoning for how it was chosen, since backers who've supported crowdfunding projects before have generally learned that an inflated, unexplained goal is a much bigger red flag for project competence than a modest, clearly justified one.
